title: Mini-window priority allocator for continuous batching (WIP)
content:
Purpose and motivation:

This note explores a hybrid scheduling primitive we
re calling the "mini-window priority allocator" for the continuous batching runtime. The goal is to get most of the latency benefits of request-level prioritization while retaining token-level coalescing efficiency and respecting long-term fairness constraints across tenants and request classes.

Why a new primitive?
- Current continuous-batching experiments show a trade-off: token-level coalescers get excellent throughput but can cause head-of-line latency variability and subtle unfairness when some requests emit few tokens and others stream long sequences.
- Pure request-level schedulers are simpler for bounded-latency SLOs but lose token-locality benefits (KV-cache hits, kernel selection stability) and often increase total GPU work per token.
- We need a design that:
  - Keeps per-token batching/coalescing to reuse KV cache & optimize kernel paths.
  - Allows latency-sensitive requests to bypass deep aggregation without starving low-priority tenants.
  - Is implementable as a scheduler layer with modest per-request state and traces for debugging.

Design goals (prioritized):
1) Latency SLO compliance for latency-classified requests (p50/p95 targets).
2) Strong short-term fairness: no tenant can monopolize GPU for extended periods.
3) Maintain high KV-cache locality and reuse kernels across batches.
4) Incremental deployability: feature flag + tracing + opt-out per customer.

Core idea (high level):
- The allocator maintains tiny time "mini-windows" (configurable, e.g., 1-4ms) during which tokens are grouped aggressively (token-level coalescing).
- Requests are tagged with a latency class (realtime, interactive, background) and a dynamic credit score.
- Each mini-window has two admission slots: a small number of low-latency fast-path slots reserved for realtime/hedged work, and an accumulation slot for bulk token coalescing.
- Within the accumulation slot we continue token-level coalescing; the fast-path allows urgent requests to be emitted earlier using a compact batch that still benefits from KV-cache where possible.

Components and state: (per-CPU / per-gpu shard)
- Window clock: continuously advances; windows overlap slightly (staggered) to reduce clumping.
- Inflight queue: per-request ring for upcoming tokens, with metadata: request-id, tenant, latency-class, sequence-length-remaining, kv-locality-key (if known), arrival_ts.
- Credit buckets: per-tenant and per-latency-class virtual-time counters (see fairness model).
- Fast-path slots: integer count configurable per window shard.
- Observability hooks: traces for window decisions, per-token tagging of which window emitted it, and cache-hit correlation.

Admission algorithm (stepwise):
1) On token arrival, place token into inflight ring and compute a prioritization score = f(latency-class, bucket-credit, kv-locality_hint).
2) At mini-window boundary: select up to fast-path-slots tokens with highest score among tokens whose requests are marked latency-sensitive and have positive bucket-credit. These form a compact fast batch (small size, often <8).
3) Remaining tokens in the window are grouped by kv-locality-key and request-age and then coalesced into the accumulation batch up to a maximum batch size. Kernel hints (e.g., attention width quantization profile) are attached based on the dominant sequence-length-distribution in the batch.
4) Emit fast-path batch immediately; emit accumulation batch after kernel selection / scheduling latency budget check.

Fairness model (virtual credits + decay):
- Each tenant has a credit counter C_t initialized to a baseline and replenished periodically (token-equivalents per second).
- When a token from tenant t is emitted on the fast-path, debit C_t by weight_fast (higher cost). For accumulation-path tokens, debit by weight_batch (lower cost).
- Credits decay/regen: C_t := min(C_max, C_t + regen_rate * dt). Tenants with low credits get deprioritized for the fast-path but still participate in accumulation batches.
- To prevent slow starvation, we implement a long-tail guarantee: if a tenant is starved on the fast-path beyond a threshold T_starve, it is allowed a boosted allotment in the next N windows.

KV-cache locality heuristics: 
- KV-cache is highly sensitive to request-context and model variant. To preserve cache hits:
  - When coalescing accumulation batches, prefer grouping tokens that share kv-locality-key (same prompt prefix or same document id) even if it slightly increases per-window latency for other tokens.
  - For fast-path slots, prefer tokens that already have warm KV entries (avoid cold-start single-token hedges that will thrash cache).
- We track a rolling estimate of KV hit probability per kv-locality-key; this metric is used by the prioritization score.

Kernel selection tie-in: 
- Batches that are mixed length (short and long sequences) force kernel variability. To reduce kernel churn:
  - Use a small lookahead within the window to pick the dominant length bucket and bias accumulation grouping toward it.
  - If a fast-path batch would otherwise cause a kernel switch that hurts throughput, downgrade that token to next window unless its latency-class preempts it.

Metrics to collect (for evaluation):
- Per-window: tokens emitted, fast-path slots used, accumulation batch size distribution, kernel-change count, KV hit rate per-batch.
- SLA metrics: p50/p95 latency by latency-class before/after changes.
- Fairness metrics: long-run token share per-tenant, slot-accumulation split, number of boosted allotments triggered.
- Resource metrics: GPU utilization, average kernel time per-token.

Experimental plan:
1) Simulated workload replay: run against recorded traces (mix of short chat completions, long streaming tasks, embedding-heavy workloads) to tune mini-window size and fast-path slot counts.
2) Small canary on dedicated capacity with 2 tenants, aggressive/unrestricted and conservative workloads to validate fairness rules.
3) Measure KV hit regression: ensure no >5% drop in KV hit-rate across representative mixes.
4) Ramp to multi-tenant cluster with telemetry and automatic rollback triggers if p95 latency for realtime class degrades.

Open questions and risks:
- How to set weights for fast-path vs accumulation debit to align with true GPU cost? Requires microbenchmarks across kernels.
- Is mini-window size stable across hardware (A100 vs H100 vs CPU fallback)? Likely need per-hardware tuning.
- Hedged requests can still cause tail amplification if many tenants mark requests as realtime. Need a backpressure or admission-control at API surface.
- Complexity: per-window stagger and overlap adds complexity to correctness and tracing; need good visualization.

Action items (next steps):
- Ravi: prototype a simulator that implements the admission algorithm and fairness model (due 2024-11-29).
- María: collect kernel microbenchmarks to estimate weight_fast vs weight_batch (due 2024-11-25).
- Ethan: add observability hooks for per-window trace ids and KV hit tagging in serving-runtime branch (PR referenced above).
- Avery: write a short experiment plan and canary rollout checklist for infra/sre review (due 2024-11-22).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a hybrid approach (not purely token-level or request-level). The micro-window abstraction is an attempt to get the best of both worlds: token reuse inside the window, and predictable low-latency fast-path for urgent requests.
- Please focus feedback on the fairness accounting (credit model), operational complexity, and any obvious attack vectors where a tenant could game credits.
